title: Undefined to Null
statement:
Write `undefinedToNull(obj)`. The argument `obj` is an object or an array, and its values may themselves be objects and arrays, nested to any depth. Return it with every `undefined` value, at every depth, turned into `null`; all other values stay exactly as they are, and no property or element is added or removed. You may change `obj` in place or build a new value.

Why it is useful: `JSON.stringify` silently drops an object property whose value is `undefined` (and writes `null` for one inside an array), so converting first makes the serialized result predictable.

JSON has no `undefined`, so each case gives `obj` as text: JSON in which `undefined` may also appear as a value. The judge turns that text into a real object or array, calls `undefinedToNull` once, and writes the returned value back as compact text in the same notation (keys in the object's own order, `undefined` spelled out wherever one is left). That text is the answer.
constraints: obj is an object or an array
Every value inside obj is null, a boolean, a number, a string, an array, an object or undefined
2 <= length of obj written as text <= 10^5
api: undefinedToNull(obj: Record<string, unknown> | unknown[]): Record<string, unknown> | unknown[]
notes:
## Intuition

`undefined` can hide anywhere inside `obj`, at any depth, so the function has to visit every value. The structure is a tree: objects and arrays are inner nodes, everything else is a leaf. A recursive walk handles it naturally: look at each value of the current container; replace it when it is `undefined`, descend into it when it is itself a container, and leave it alone otherwise. `Object.keys` lists the keys of an object and the indexes of an array alike, so one loop serves both. (The brute force uses `JSON.stringify` with a replacer that turns `undefined` into `null`, then parses the text back.)

## Approach

1. For each `key` of `Object.keys(obj)`, read `value = obj[key]`.
2. If `value === undefined`, write `null` in its place.
3. Otherwise, if `value` is a non-null object (a plain object or an array), call `undefinedToNull(value)` to clean it in place.
4. Leave every other value as it is, and return `obj` after the loop.

## Example 1, step by step

`obj` is `{ a: undefined, b: 3 }`, so `Object.keys(obj)` is `["a", "b"]`.

- `key = "a"`: `value` is `undefined`, so `obj.a = null`.
- `key = "b"`: `value` is `3`, neither `undefined` nor a container, so nothing changes.
- Return `obj`, now `{ a: null, b: 3 }`, written as `{"a":null,"b":3}`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n), where n is the number of values inside `obj`: each is looked at once.
- Space: O(d) for the recursion, where d is the nesting depth; the conversion happens in place.

## Pitfalls

- `if (!value)` also catches `0`, `false`, `""` and `null`; compare with `=== undefined`.
- `typeof null` is `"object"`, so test `value !== null` before recursing, or `Object.keys(null)` throws.
- `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))` without a replacer **drops** object properties holding `undefined` instead of keeping them as `null`.
- Deleting the key instead of assigning `null` changes the shape; the key must stay.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `obj` | the object or array being cleaned in place |
| `key` | a property name, or an array index as a string |
| `value` | `obj[key]`, the value under that key |

narration.1: undefinedToNull cleans one object or array in place and calls itself for nested ones.
narration.2: Object.keys lists property names for objects and indexes for arrays, so one loop handles both.
narration.3: Read the value stored under this key.
narration.4: Only undefined is replaced; 0, false, empty strings and null stay as they are.
narration.5: Write null where undefined was, keeping the key.
narration.6: A non-null object is a nested container (typeof null is also "object", hence the extra check).
narration.7: Recurse to clean the nested object or array in place.
narration.10: Every value has been visited; return the cleaned obj.
